Hi kenji as a peruvian fan is really great to see some of our dishes done by you, hope you give more of them a chance. Just wanted to  gush about ceviche's history since as a kid born in the coast, for me ceviche is the best and most balanced peruvian dish. And I find that the evolution the recipe has gone trough is really fascinating and encapsulates the mix of backgrounds peruvian cousine offers. 
As some other commenter has pointed out, most researchers, agree that ceviche (also written as cebiche, but i think v looks prettier than b) has it's roots in moche culture, where the've traced consumption of raw fish, marinated in critics native to the land like tumbo. With the colonization from spain, the citric of choice became lime (which in Peru we call limon, which is translated as lemon), and onion got introduced as a core component of the dish. 

As you said, beyond that, the other parts of the recipe are more of the chef or regions choice. I've found in recipes that most cooks agree on culantro (which I understand is translated as cilantro or coriander but some commenters and quick google searches have gotten me confused and wondering if cilantro and culantro are different herbs), garlic, onion and chilies (which is another rabbit hole of peruvian variants, we normally use a red one, quite small called aji limo, but it also comes in different colors like orange or purple). Lots of time we either let the aromatics infuse in the lime juice by letting them soak for sometime in the juice, or we blend it all along with some fish leftovers to make the famous "leche de tigre". Which use to only refer to the leftover juice of ceviche that had aquired some fish taste to it, but it is now made from scratch. The choice of either infused lime, or "leche de tigre" (translated to tiger's milk for anyone interested) seems to be a north vs capital (lima) difference.

 But other people (like myself) also add ginger and celery (celery is definitly the most controversial aromatic, some people swear that I doesn't belong in ceviche, I find that it balances out the flavour quite well), and quite important for northean ceviche MSG! lots of houses use MSG under the brand name of ajinomoto, but as we all know MSG usage is looked down upon by some. And more people are beginning to experiment, using passion fruit as the citric, using salmon, bonito or trout instead of white fishes or adding soy sauce, green onion and sesame oil to give it an asian profile

On that note, most ceviche specially nowadays is way closer to a sashimi than the original marinated fish. When you look to recipes from the 80s (I have a cookbook from my grandmom) it called for up to 4-6 hours of marination, in an understanding that the longer it was in the juice it cooked the fish more, thereby making it safe. I think the understanding that the "cooking" does not eliminate patogens has reduced the necesity of longer marination. But I also wonder if the importance of japanese inmigration in peruvian culinary tradition has impacted our understanding of good ceviche as in, as fresh as the fish gets (that applies both to the catch, but also the time it has entered the lime juice). It has certainly developed a brother of ceviche which is tiradito. Very slim cuts of fish (in practice sashimi), served with the mentioned infused juice, omitting the onions and also accompanied by a sauce  (the most popular ones are made from aji amarillo, rocoto and olives). I cannot recommend tiradito enough although I have no clue if it is served in the us or other parts of the world

And that is just the ceviche itself, the list of sides the dish has is long and again depends heavily in region. Sweet potatoes, mandioca or tapioca either fried or boiled, boiled corn (choclo), fried corn (cancha, it is a different variant of corn, that also has a different variant called cancha chulpi, my preffered one if I'm honest, it is way crunchier), fried plantains (chifles) and lettuce are the most common all trought the country. Zarandaja a boiled bean and tortitas de choclo, are very typical in the north coast, while in the tropical part, they also serve ceviche with rice, and the local chili variant (charapita)

Hope that the long comment shows just how much layers and history there is in such a simple dish at the end of the day, and that in part is what I love about our food and people. Hope anyone finds some of the information as fascinating as I do, sorry if my english is chopped in some places!!!

I think it's a great representation of the history of the country/area. The indigenous population would marinate fish with passion fruit. Then when the Spanish arrived, Moorish women with them brought lemons and limes to South America, which is how lime began to be used. Then when Japanese immigrants arrived in Peru, they perfected ceviche by cutting it in larger pieces and only marinating the fish for 10-15 minutes instead of hours.

Mexican ceviche is mostly citrus based marinated, usually with green lime, while there's a red sauce version it uses tomate+clam+spices juice, being "Clamato" the most popular brand, but never with ketchup, some places find it even offensive if you put it on ceviche. The red ceviche in Mexico is popular on certain parts of the Pacific coast and looks a bit like a stew since it's really watery. The most traditional Mexican ceviche is similar to Peruvian but adds chiles + cucumber and it doesn't contain corn, olive oil or the sweet potato side, is mostly eaten on "tostadas" which is a dehydrated corn tortilla, sometimes even fried as well. Both versions are delicious and both must be prepared with raw, fresh fish. Great video!
